usage: Reads exactly like this on a Korean clothing tag; spoken as '면 백 퍼센트'.
순(純, pure) + 면; the label word on bedding, towels, and baby clothes.
면 + item is the normal way to say what a thing is made of — no 으로 needed.
소재 = material/fabric; staff lean on this word when describing what clothes are made from.
examples: 이거 면이에요?
Is this cotton?
The shortest, most useful tag-check question; 이거 + 명사 + 이에요? identifies a material.
여름엔 면 소재가 시원해서 좋아요.
In summer cotton material is nice because it's cool.
시원하다 pairs naturally with breathable fabric; -아서 here gives the reason you like it.
면 100%라서 빨면 좀 줄어들 수 있어요.
It's 100% cotton, so it may shrink a bit when you wash it.
줄어들다 (shrink) is the real warning shop staff give about cotton; -라서 links the cause.
nuance: 면 is the Sino-Korean word for cotton fabric (한자 綿, 'cotton/silk-floss'), and it papers Korean clothing, bedding, and towel tags. The near-synonym trap is 솜: 면 is the woven cloth you wear, while 솜 is the fluffy stuffing/batting packed inside a duvet or padded jacket — same raw fiber, totally different product, so a 솜이불 (stuffed quilt) is not a 면 garment. Register is neutral; everyone from shop staff to friends just says 면. The big English-speaker pitfall is the homophones: 면 also means 'noodles' (麵) and 'side/aspect' (面), so only the shopping-vs-food context separates them. Another trap is over-marking the material — beginners say 면으로 만든 티셔츠, but natural Korean is simply 면 티셔츠, sticking the material straight onto the noun.

mistakes: Saying 솜 when you mean the fabric — 솜 is the fluffy cotton stuffing inside padding or quilts, while the woven cloth you wear is 면. Ask for a 면 티셔츠, not a 솜 티셔츠.
Adding 으로 만든 every time (면으로 만든 바지). It is grammatical but heavy; native speech just says 면 바지, 면 티셔츠 with the material glued onto the noun.
Reading the tag homophone wrong: 면 on a menu is 'noodles' (麵), not cotton. Let the clothes-vs-food context tell you which 면 it is.

usage: What you ask for when you don't want fake; 진짜 = real, the everyday opposite of 가짜.
인조(人造, man-made) + 가죽; the formal label term, more precise than the casual 가짜 가죽.
소(cow) + 가죽; the most common leather for bags and shoes, named by animal.
가죽 + item is the standard pattern for naming a leather thing.
examples: 이거 진짜 가죽이에요?
Is this real leather?
The single most useful market question; 진짜 in front flags that you doubt it's genuine.
가죽 제품은 비 오는 날 조심해야 해요.
You have to be careful with leather products on rainy days.
조심하다 + -아야 하다 gives practical 'you must' care advice you'll actually hear.
진짜 가죽치고 가격이 너무 싼데요?
For real leather, the price is awfully cheap, isn't it?
N치고 = 'for / considering a N'; -ㄴ데요 softly voices polite suspicion about a too-good deal.
nuance: 가죽 is a native Korean word covering all animal leather, and shops split it into 진짜 가죽 (real) versus 인조가죽 or 합성피혁 (synthetic) on the tag. The synonym line that trips up English speakers is 피부 vs 가죽: both can translate as 'skin,' but 피부 is living human/animal skin and skincare, whereas 가죽 is the tanned material made from a hide — you have nice 피부, but you buy a 가죽 가방. Register is neutral; casual speech freely says 가짜 가죽 for fake, while labels prefer 인조가죽. Natural collocations are 진짜 가죽, 소가죽, 가죽 지갑/가방/구두, and the verb 가죽이 갈라지다 (the leather cracks). The pitfall: vendors at markets like Dongdaemun call PU/synthetic 가죽 loosely, so always confirm with 진짜 가죽이에요? before paying a leather price.

Assuming any item called 가죽 is genuine. Sellers apply 가죽 to PU/synthetic too, so pin it down with 진짜 가죽이에요? or look for the label word 인조가죽.
Saying 가죽으로 every time; for naming an item, native speech just compounds it: 가죽 지갑, 가죽 구두, 가죽 소파.

usage: Reads on sweater and coat tags; pronounced '울 백 퍼센트'.
울 + item; the warm winter coat people line up to buy for Korean winters.
양(sheep, 羊) + 모(hair, 毛); the technical word printed on care labels, not used in chat.
니트 (knit) + 울 to pin down the material of the sweater.
examples: 이 코트 울이에요?
Is this coat wool?
Basic material check; 명사 + 이에요? is your all-purpose 'is this made of ___?' question.
울은 따뜻하지만 물세탁하면 안 돼요.
Wool is warm, but you mustn't machine-/water-wash it.
-지만 contrasts the upside with the catch; 물세탁하면 안 되다 = washing with water is not allowed.
울 스웨터는 드라이클리닝 맡기는 게 좋아요.
It's best to take wool sweaters to the dry cleaner.
맡기다 = to entrust/drop off; V-는 게 좋다 = 'it's best to' for recommended care.
nuance: 울 is the loanword for wool (straight from English 'wool'), and it dominates Korean winter-clothing tags. Its register-twin is 양모 (羊毛, literally 'sheep-hair'): same material, but 양모 is the bookish label word on care tags while 울 is what anyone says out loud — call a sweater 양모 니트 in conversation and it sounds like you read it off a box. A second contrast worth knowing is 캐시미어 (cashmere), a pricier, softer goat fiber often blended with 울; a tag reading 울 70 캐시미어 30 is a blend, which is why asking 울 몇 퍼센트예요? signals you know quality. The classic English-speaker pitfall is spelling/sound: 울 (wool) versus 월 (month, as in 1월) — one vowel apart and totally different, so don't write 월 코트.

mistakes: Writing 월 (month) for 울 (wool). They look and sound close but 월 is the calendar word (예: 12월), while the fabric is 울. A '월 코트' makes no sense.
Calling 양모 in everyday conversation. 양모 (羊毛) is the formal label term; spoken Korean uses 울. Save 양모 for reading care tags.
Machine-washing 울 because you skipped the label — real wool felts and shrinks, so it needs 드라이클리닝 or gentle hand washing, never a hot wash.

usage: 실크 + item; scarves are the most common silk buy, often as a gift.
On the tag of nicer blouses and scarves; spoken '실크 백 퍼센트'.
Native term you meet around 한복 (hanbok) and traditional craft goods.
같다 (to be like) turns it into a texture description rather than the actual material.
examples: 이 스카프 실크예요?
Is this scarf silk?
Quick material check; the most natural opener before you ask the price or feel it.
실크라서 손세탁만 가능해요.
Since it's silk, only hand-washing is possible.
-라서 gives the reason; 손세탁만 가능하다 = the standard care limit for delicate silk.
선물용으로 실크 스카프 하나 살까 해요.
I'm thinking of buying a silk scarf as a gift.
V-(으)ㄹ까 하다 = 'thinking of doing'; 선물용 = for-gift purpose, a useful shopping word.
nuance: 실크 is the everyday loanword for silk and rules modern speech and department-store tags. Its synonym is the native 비단, but the line is register and setting, not meaning: 비단 carries a traditional, almost literary flavor and lives around 한복, 보자기, and craft fairs, so saying 비단 스카프 at a glossy mall sounds quaint even though staff understand it — there they expect 실크. The texture that sells it is 부드럽다 (soft) and a smooth 촉감 (feel/touch), and a near-miss word is 새틴/satin, a weave that can be silk or polyester, so 실크 같다 ('silk-like') is how you hedge when you're unsure it's the real fiber. The pitfall for English speakers is care: 'silk' feels washable in English, but real 실크 almost always needs 손세탁 (hand washing) or dry cleaning, never a machine.

mistakes: Saying 비단 in a modern department store. Staff get it, but 비단 (native, traditional) belongs with 한복 and crafts; for a mall blouse everyone says 실크.
Expecting to machine-wash 실크. Real silk needs 손세탁 or 드라이클리닝; tossing it in the washer ruins the fiber and the shine.
Confusing 실크 (the actual fiber) with 실크 같다 ('silky'). The 같다 form only describes texture — a 실크 같은 블라우스 may really be polyester.

usage: 용기 = container; the everyday word for tupperware-type food boxes.
플라스틱 + item to state what it is made of.
전자레인지 + 용(用, for-use); the spec to check before microwaving a container.
쓰레기 = trash; relevant because Korea's recycling sorting is strict.
examples: 이거 플라스틱이에요?
Is this plastic?
Fast material check; 이거 + 명사 + 이에요? works for any 'what's this made of?' moment.
이 용기 전자레인지에 돌려도 돼요?
Can I microwave this container?
돌리다 (to run/spin) is the casual verb for 'microwave it'; -아도 돼요? asks permission.
저렴한 건 플라스틱이고 비싼 건 유리예요.
The cheap ones are plastic and the expensive ones are glass.
-는 ... -고 ... contrasts two product tiers by price, a common in-store comparison.
nuance: 플라스틱 is the all-purpose loanword for plastic, covering containers, chairs, and packaging — there is no everyday native synonym, so this borrowed word does all the work. Two contrasts matter when shopping: against 유리 (glass), where 플라스틱 is light and unbreakable but seen as less hygienic and not always microwave-safe; and against 비닐, which English lumps in as 'plastic' too but Korean keeps separate — 비닐 is thin film/sheeting (the 비닐봉지 plastic bag, plastic wrap), while 플라스틱 is rigid molded plastic (the box, the chair). Because Korea enforces 분리수거 (waste sorting) strictly, this word matters beyond the store. The English-speaker pitfall is pronunciation: it is not the two-beat English 'plastic' but a clean four-syllable 플·라·스·틱, and calling a 비닐봉지 a 플라스틱 봉지 will get a puzzled look.

mistakes: Calling a plastic bag a 플라스틱 봉지. Thin film bags and wrap are 비닐 (비닐봉지, 비닐); 플라스틱 is rigid molded plastic like a box or chair.
Microwaving any 플라스틱 without checking. Only 전자레인지용 (microwave-safe) plastic is rated for heat — ask 전자레인지에 돌려도 돼요? first.
Pronouncing it as English 'plastic.' Korean is 플라스틱 with four clear syllables; squashing it makes it hard to understand.

usage: 컵 = cup; the standard drinking glass, written as one word.
Marketed as heat-safe and more hygienic than plastic ones.
강화(强化, strengthened) + 유리; what you buy as a phone screen protector or tough cookware.
(으)로 되다 = 'be made of'; a natural way to state material — 유리로 된 컵.
examples: 이 컵 유리예요?
Is this cup glass?
Plain material check; 명사 + 이에요? is the all-purpose 'is this ___?' question.
유리라서 깨질까 봐 걱정돼요.
Since it's glass, I'm worried it might break.
깨지다 + V-(으)ㄹ까 봐 = worry that something might happen; -라서 supplies the reason.
휴대폰에 강화유리 하나 붙이려고요.
I'm planning to put a tempered glass on my phone.
붙이다 = to stick on; -(으)려고요 states your shopping intention politely.
nuance: 유리 is glass as a material (Sino-Korean 琉璃, originally a word for colored glass/lapis), used for cups, containers, windows, and 강화유리 (tempered glass) screen protectors. Shoppers constantly weigh it against 플라스틱: 유리 is heavier and breakable but prized as cleaner and microwave/oven-safe. The synonym confusions for English speakers are two: 거울 (mirror) is a separate word — a mirror is made from 유리 but you call it a 거울, not 유리; and 잔, which is the counter/word for a glass-as-a-serving (a 와인 잔, '한 잔 더' = one more glass to drink) rather than the substance. Common collocations are 유리컵, 유리병, 유리 용기, 강화유리, and 유리가 깨지다 (the glass breaks). One more trap: 유리 is also a very common woman's given name, so in a sentence about a person it may be a name, not the material.

Using 유리 for 'a glass' you drink from. The serving/counter word is 잔 (한 잔 더 주세요); 유리 is the raw material, 유리컵 is the physical cup.
Forgetting 유리 doubles as a girl's name. '유리가 예뻐요' could praise the glass or the person named Yuri — context decides.

usage: The single most practical phrase — say it before buying earrings, watches, or belts.
재질(材質) = material/composition; staff use it when describing what a product is made of.
프레임 (frame) for glasses, beds, or furniture.
(으)로 되다 = 'be made of'; 금속으로 된 부분 = the metal part.
examples: 이거 금속이에요?
Is this metal?
Quick material check; useful for jewelry where you may react to certain metals.
저 금속 알레르기 있어서 다른 거 없어요?
I have a metal allergy, so don't you have something else?
있어서 (-아서, 'because I have') chains the reason to a polite request for an alternative.
금속 부분이 녹스니까 물기를 닦아 주세요.
The metal part rusts, so please wipe off the moisture.
녹슬다 = to rust; -니까 gives the reason for the -아 주세요 request to wipe it dry.
nuance: 금속 is the general category word for metal (Sino-Korean 金屬, 金 'gold/metal' + 屬 'belong to,' i.e. 'things in the metal family'). It is the umbrella; for a specific metal Koreans name it directly — 금 (gold, 金), 은 (silver, 銀), 철 (iron/steel, 鐵), 스테인리스 (stainless), 알루미늄 (aluminum) — so the key contrast to internalize is 금속 ≠ 금: 금속 is metal-in-general, while 금 is specifically gold (and a single character of the very same compound). The most useful real-life collocation is 금속 알레르기 (metal allergy), exactly what you say when earrings or a watch make your skin react. Other natural partners: 금속 재질, 금속 프레임, 금속이 녹슬다 (metal rusts). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 금 ('metal' sounds gold-ish) when you mean any metal, or using 철 (iron specifically) as if it meant metal generally.

Using 철 (iron/steel) as a catch-all for metal. 철 is one specific metal; if you don't know which one, say 금속.

usage: 고무 + 장갑; the dishwashing/cleaning gloves in every Korean kitchen.
고무 + 줄(string); also the stretchy elastic in a waistband.
밑창 = sole of a shoe; non-slip rubber soles are a selling point.
재질 = material; how staff describe what something is made of.
examples: 설거지할 때 고무장갑 끼는 게 좋아요.
It's good to wear rubber gloves when washing dishes.
끼다 = to put on (gloves); V-는 게 좋다 = 'it's good to,' the most common use of 고무.
이 신발 밑창이 고무라서 안 미끄러워요.
This shoe's sole is rubber, so it isn't slippery.
미끄럽다 = slippery; -라서 ties the rubber sole to the non-slip result.
바지 허리가 고무줄이라 진짜 편해요.
The waist of these pants is elastic, so it's really comfy.
고무줄 here = the waistband elastic; -(이)라 gives the casual reason, 편하다 = comfortable.
nuance: 고무 means rubber and feels fully native even though it entered Korean as a loanword (via Dutch/Japanese 'gom'). It shows up most in 고무장갑 (rubber gloves), an absolute staple you'll grab at any 마트 or 다이소, and in 고무줄, which usefully covers both a 'rubber band' and the stretchy 'elastic' in clothing waistbands — context decides which. The synonym/pitfall to watch is footwear: rubber rain boots are 장화, not 고무 신발, even though they're literally rubber, because Korean names them by function, not material. Likewise the bouncy 'rubber' of a tire is just 타이어, and a rubber eraser is 지우개 — you rarely say 고무 for these finished objects. Natural collocations: 고무장갑 끼다, 고무 밑창, 고무줄로 묶다 (tie with a rubber band), 고무가 늘어나다 (the rubber stretches).

usage: 그릇 = bowl/dish; the typical ceramic tableware.
컵 + 도자기 to pin down the material.
전통(傳統) = traditional; sold as Korean craft and souvenir pieces.
제품 = product; a category sign you'll see at homeware shops.
examples: 이 그릇 도자기예요?
Is this dish ceramic?
Quick material check; matters because it affects price, weight, and microwave-safety.
도자기는 떨어뜨리면 바로 깨져요.
Ceramic breaks right away if you drop it.
떨어뜨리다 = to drop; -면 ... 바로 = 'as soon as / right away,' the fragility warning.
인사동에서 예쁜 도자기 컵을 하나 샀어요.
I bought a pretty ceramic cup in Insadong.
Insadong is the go-to spot for traditional 도자기; 하나 = 'one (of them)' counts the item.
nuance: 도자기 is the word for ceramics/pottery, a Sino-Korean compound (陶瓷器: 陶 'earthenware' + 瓷 'porcelain' + 器 'vessel') that literally bundles the two fired-clay families into 'fired-clay ware.' It runs from everyday dishes to prized craft pieces sold in places like Insadong, often labeled 전통 도자기. The synonym map is worth knowing: 도자기 is the umbrella, while 도기 (陶器) is coarser earthenware and 자기 (瓷器) is fine porcelain/china; for traditional Korean wares you'll also hear 백자 (white porcelain) and 청자 (celadon) as named subtypes. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: don't confuse glossy 도자기 with 유리 (glass) just because both shine — they're different materials and break differently; and don't microwave 도자기 that has gold or silver trim, because the metallic paint can spark. Common collocations: 도자기 그릇, 도자기 컵, 도자기가 깨지다, 도자기를 굽다 (to fire pottery).

usage: 텀블러 = tumbler; the insulated bottle everyone carries.
냄비 = pot; a common upgrade from coated pans because nothing peels.
Very common spoken contraction of 스테인리스 — you'll hear it shouted at markets.
식기(食器) = tableware; the metal bowls and spoons used in many homes.
examples: 이 텀블러 스테인리스예요?
Is this tumbler stainless?
Material check; matters for heat retention and whether it'll rust.
스테인리스라서 보온이 잘 돼요.
Since it's stainless, it keeps heat well.
보온(保溫) = heat retention; -라서 links the material to its main selling point.
아주머니, 이거 스뎅이에요?
Ma'am, is this stainless?
스뎅 is the natural spoken form you'd actually use at a market stall; 아주머니 addresses the vendor.
nuance: 스테인리스 is the loanword for stainless steel, everywhere in Korean kitchens — 텀블러, 냄비, bowls, spoons. Two register notes are essential. First, the full English 'stainless steel' gets trimmed: Korean drops 스틸 and says just 스테인리스, and in casual market speech it contracts even further to 스뎅, so recognizing 스뎅 is genuinely useful when an 아주머니 uses it. Second, the synonym/pitfall is other shiny metals: not every gleaming pan is 스테인리스 — much lighter cookware is 알루미늄 (aluminum), and coated nonstick pans look metallic but their coating (코팅) peels, which is the very durability argument that sells 스테인리스. Natural collocations: 스테인리스 냄비/텀블러/식기, 보온이 잘 되다, 코팅이 안 벗겨지다 (the coating doesn't peel), 녹이 안 슬다 (it doesn't rust). The pitfall for English speakers is over-spelling it as 스테인리스 스틸 and not recognizing the slang 스뎅.

usage: The fabric tote you use instead of plastic; very common in Korea.
소파 = sofa; the in-store either/or against a 가죽 (leather) sofa.
(으)로 되다 = 'be made of'; 천으로 된 가방 = a fabric bag.
부드럽다 = soft; describing texture while you shop.
examples: 이 소파 천이에요, 가죽이에요?
Is this sofa fabric or leather?
A standard either/or question when furniture shopping; 천 vs 가죽 is the core split.
천 가방은 가벼워서 장 볼 때 좋아요.
A cloth bag is light, so it's good for grocery shopping.
장(을) 보다 = to do grocery shopping; -아서 gives the reason it's handy.
천이 얇아서 비치는데 다른 색 없어요?
The fabric is thin and see-through; don't you have another color?
얇다 = thin; 비치다 = to show through, a real clothing complaint, -는데 softens the request.
nuance: 천 is the native general word for cloth/fabric — any soft woven textile, as opposed to 가죽 (leather), 플라스틱, or 금속. It's the everyday way to ask what something is made of: 천이에요, 가죽이에요? The synonym layer to sort out: 천 is the broadest term, 옷감 specifically means dressmaking fabric/'material for clothes,' and 원단 is the trade/industry word for bolt fabric you'd hear at a fabric market like Dongdaemun — so 천 is what you say in normal life, 원단 is shoptalk. Crucially, 천 is the umbrella, while 면 (cotton), 울 (wool), and 실크 (silk) are specific kinds of 천, so don't say 천 when you actually mean cotton. The headline English-speaker pitfall is the homophone: 천 is also the number 1,000 (千), spelled and pronounced identically — '천 원' is a thousand won, '천으로 된 가방' is a cloth bag, and only context separates them. Collocations: 천 가방, 천 소파, 천이 얇다/두껍다, 천을 자르다 (cut fabric).

Using 원단 in casual talk. 원단 is the trade word for bolt fabric at a fabric market; in everyday speech just say 천.

usage: On the tags of cheaper clothing and sportswear; spoken '합성섬유 백 퍼센트'.
The most common specific 합성섬유 actually named on labels.
천연(天然) = natural; the opposite category — cotton, wool, silk.
소재 = material; how the fabric type is described on a spec line.
examples: 이 옷 합성섬유예요?
Is this garment synthetic fiber?
Material check; tells you how it'll wash, breathe, and wrinkle.
합성섬유라서 잘 안 구겨져요.
Since it's synthetic, it doesn't wrinkle easily.
구겨지다 = to get wrinkled; -라서 ties wrinkle-resistance to the synthetic material.
천연섬유가 좋아요, 합성섬유가 좋아요?
Do you prefer natural fibers or synthetic ones?
The basic fabric either/or when shopping; parallel A가 좋아요, B가 좋아요? offers a choice.
nuance: 합성섬유 is the umbrella term for man-made fabrics — a Sino-Korean compound (合成纖維: 合成 'synthesized/combined' + 纖維 'fiber'), literally 'synthesized fiber.' On labels its named members are things like 폴리에스터 (polyester), 나일론 (nylon), and 아크릴 (acrylic), so 폴리에스터 is a specific kind of 합성섬유, not a different category. The sharp contrast to lock in is 합성섬유 ↔ 천연섬유 (天然纖維, 'natural fiber'): they sit on opposite sides of the care label, with 면/울/실크 in the 천연 column. The practical trade-off — and the reason this word is worth knowing in humid Korea — is that 합성섬유 resists wrinkles and dries fast but breathes poorly, so summer wear in it can feel sticky while sportswear uses it on purpose for stretch and quick-dry. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 합성섬유 as automatically 'bad/cheap'; it's a neutral category, and registering it as the opposite of 천연섬유 (rather than as an insult) keeps your tag-reading accurate.
